selection_method.unit: independently searchable source subject rather than proposed index heading
principles: Retain principal subjects and significant localized or subsidiary subjects even when confined to one passage.
Split subjects when a reader could plausibly seek one without the other or when a combined label would overstate page support.
Retain named people, institutions, works, and events only when the chapter analyzes them, uses them as sustained explanatory cases, or makes them independently useful to scholarly readers.
Use optional only for defensible supplemental access whose absence would not materially reduce usefulness.
Do not use density calibration to set the subject count or priority.

page_review.word_count_method: Counted the owned-page body text extracted with Poppler pdftotext -layout after removing running headers, printed page numbers, and the chapter-title display, and rejoining alphabetic end-of-line hyphenations. Substantive block quotations and numeric tokens were included; context pages and absent endnotes were excluded.

page_accounting.summary: Carries forward sansculotte subsistence grievances, the Montagnard struggle with the enragés, and Marat's assassination.
Establishes Robespierre's entry into the Committee, emergency legislation, and suspension of the newly ratified constitution.
Defines the July 1793 military, civil-war, and Parisian political crisis and the perceived absence of effective government.
Describes the Committee's developing leadership and the collapse of resistance in Normandy, Brittany, and Bordeaux.
Traces the surrender of Marseilles, Toulon's alliance with Britain, and the rise of Hébertist popular leadership in Paris.
Sets out the radical program of maximum prices, revolutionary armies, mass mobilization, and terror amid worsening subsistence conditions.
Narrates the 4–5 September popular mobilization, immediate emergency decrees, and enactment of the Law of Suspects.
Covers social policing, the General Maximum, political trials, suppression of the enragés, and formalization of Revolutionary Government.
Introduces the Terror's scale, famous Paris victims, and the decision to punish Lyons as an exceptional example.
Details the destruction decree and mass executions at Lyons, then the decisive republican assault at Toulon.
Compares repression at Toulon, Marseilles, and Bordeaux and introduces the central review of Carrier's Nantes terror.
Follows the republican counteroffensive in the Vendée and the rebels' failed northern campaign toward British aid.
Describes Savenay, the infernal columns, disputed mass mortality, and Carrier's shootings and drownings at Nantes.
Explains Carrier's recall, the locally improvised phase of terror, revolutionary armies, watch committees, and certificates of civisme.
Reassesses total mortality, social composition, regional concentration, and introduces Fouché's religious terror in the Nièvre.
Traces Fouché's civic religion, the republican calendar, and the spread of dechristianizing iconoclasm.
Details festivals, clerical renunciation, and the Paris Commune's transformation of Notre-Dame into a Temple of Reason.
Shows rural backlash, Robespierre's opposition to atheistic excess, formal protection of worship, and continuing nationwide church closure.
Presents dechristianizing disorder as a spur to the Law of 14 Frimaire and maps its centralized administrative chain.
Explains revolutionary government as wartime rule, the slow curbing of representatives, and initial problems enforcing the Maximum.
Analyzes nationwide price administration, the Subsistence Commission, black markets, military purchasing, and assignat recovery.
Covers the forced loan, the largely unrealized Ventôse redistribution, and the Terror's unplanned, self-perpetuating character.
Introduces the Indulgent campaign, Robespierre's and Danton's temporary alignment, and the Indies Company corruption allegations.
Traces Collot's defense of terror, abolition of the justice committee, Fabre's exposure, and Robespierre's break with the Indulgents.
Describes revived Hébertist agitation for insurrection amid malfunctioning price controls and popular hardship.
Narrates the political prosecution and execution of the Hébertists and explains the sansculottes' failure to defend them.
Explains sansculotte exhaustion and absorption into state offices, the purge of the Commune, and terror's transfer to firmer governmental control.
Opens the next chapter by asking what terror was for after its popular architects had been destroyed or neutralized.
Carries the transition into Robespierre's program of republican virtue and the coming prosecution of the Indulgents.

used to identify the intellectual unit but excluded from the body-word denominator

unavailable_regions.effect: No note text was counted or used as evidence; body-text treatment remained inspectable.

reader_tasks.description: Explain why military danger, civil war, shortages, and popular pressure made terror politically compelling in summer and September 1793.
Distinguish the locally improvised autumn Terror from the centralized Revolutionary Government established under the Law of 14 Frimaire.
Compare the causes, defeat, and differentiated repression of Bordeaux, Marseilles, Toulon, and Lyons.
Trace the destruction of the Vendéan field army and distinguish combat losses, infernal-column violence, judicial repression, and the Nantes drownings.
Assess the Terror's approximate death toll, social composition, and strong concentration in rebellion and frontier zones.
Explain how the Law of Suspects, watch committees, certificates of civisme, and mass detention made suspicion an administrative system.
Explain how the General Maximum, Subsistence Commission, forced loan, and Ventôse laws combined economic control with popular politics.
Trace dechristianization from provincial initiatives through Parisian festivals and church closures to Robespierre's resistance and the freedom-of-worship decree.
Explain how representatives on mission and revolutionary armies first expanded local terror and were later subordinated or abolished by central government.
Reconstruct the conflict among Hébertists, Indulgents, and the governing committees without treating allegations of foreign conspiracy as established fact.
Explain why the sansculottes did not defend Hébert and how paid participation and committee service absorbed activists into the state apparatus.
Evaluate Doyle's interpretation that terror emerged from circumstances, escaped any single actor's control, and became harsher after passing from popular to governmental hands.

subjects.label: Jacobin Republic: crisis of July 1793
subjects.meaning: The simultaneous coalition invasion, civil wars, military reverses, and unstable politics in Paris that made July 1793 the Republic's lowest point.
subjects.stance: Treat the crisis as real and multidimensional, not as a later pretext invented solely to justify repression.

evidence.evidence_summary: Coalition forces held French territory, Mainz had fallen, the Vendée remained dangerous, and several southern cities resisted the Convention.
Factional struggle and fears of hidden enemies destabilized Paris while a Committee member publicly lamented the lack of government.

subjects.label: Committee of Public Safety: consolidation of executive leadership
subjects.meaning: The Committee's evolution from an important executive committee into the directing center of wartime mobilization and administration.
subjects.stance: Do not call it an undisputed formal government before the later revolutionary-government arrangements; Doyle stresses both its early limits and its effective leadership.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Committee was criticized for weak government even as Danton unsuccessfully proposed recognizing it as the provisional government.
With military specialists added, it led an unprecedented mobilization that overcame the 1793 crisis despite lacking undisputed executive authority.
The Law of 14 Frimaire vested internal administration and police direction in the Committee under the Convention's superior authority.

subjects.label: Republican military command: political reliability versus competence
subjects.meaning: The replacement of experienced but socially suspect commanders by politically reliable sansculottes, exemplified by Biron and Rossignol.
subjects.stance: Doyle presents political vetting as damaging when it elevated an incompetent commander, while later operations still depended on varied regular and volunteer forces.

evidence.evidence_summary: Biron was removed despite success because of his former title and replaced by the politically dependable but militarily inept Rossignol.
Rossignol later commanded Parisian volunteers during the renewed republican campaign in the Vendée.

subjects.label: Federalist revolts: collapse and differentiated repression
subjects.meaning: The rapid or protracted defeat of the heterogeneous provincial revolts labeled Federalist and the sharply unequal punishments imposed afterward.
subjects.stance: Preserve Doyle's quotation-marked and differentiated usage: these movements were not one coherent ideological or military bloc, and Paris treated them very differently.

evidence.evidence_summary: Norman and Breton resistance disintegrated quickly, whereas Bordeaux's surrender was delayed and its earlier propaganda invited harsher retaliation.
Marseilles capitulated under military and subsistence pressure, while Toulon chose foreign protection and royal proclamation.
Repression ranged from mass killing at Lyons and Toulon to more regular and comparatively restrained tribunals in Marseilles and Bordeaux.

subjects.label: Bordeaux: Federalist collapse and limited Terror
subjects.meaning: The dissolution of Bordeaux's Popular Commission, hesitant restoration of Convention authority, and comparatively restrained subsequent repression.
subjects.stance: The city was culpable in Parisian eyes for propaganda and attempted coordination, but its Terror was much less severe than the rhetoric of its representatives suggested.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Popular Commission dissolved under military threats and food shortages, but hostile crowds initially forced representatives to withdraw.
Jacobin institutions reappeared before Tallien entered, yet he judged their renewed unity to rest largely on fear and hunger.
The local military commission acquitted many suspects and executed relatively few until Jullien intensified repression in mid-1794.

subjects.label: Marseilles: surrender and comparatively regulated repression
subjects.meaning: The port's collapse under blockade, food crisis, factional division, and approaching republican troops, followed by a formal tribunal with substantial acquittals.
subjects.stance: Distinguish the treasonous appeal for British assistance from the more extreme decision at Toulon, and distinguish Marseilles's tribunal from mass reprisals elsewhere.

evidence.evidence_summary: Blockade, bread riots, and Carteaux's advance split the sections between surrender and collaboration with Britain.
A procedurally careful tribunal tried hundreds and acquitted nearly half, making repression milder than at Lyons or Toulon.

subjects.label: Toulon: foreign occupation, reconquest, and repression
subjects.meaning: Toulon's acceptance of British protection and royalism, the siege and republican recovery of the naval base, and severe reprisals after evacuation.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats admission of coalition forces and loss of the fleet as exceptionally grave, while noting strategic necessity limited total destruction.

evidence.evidence_summary: Refugee atrocity reports and fear of republican conquest helped the sections accept British protection and proclaim Louis XVII.
Capture of harbor heights forced an immediate coalition evacuation after a siege lasting several months.
Republicans executed armed rebels without trial and hundreds more through a commission, while preserving the strategically indispensable naval base.

subjects.label: Lyons: exemplary destruction and mass repression
subjects.meaning: The decision to make prolonged Lyonnais resistance an example through symbolic destruction, special tribunals, shootings, and continued executions.
subjects.stance: Doyle contrasts Couthon's attempted clemency with the central demand for vengeance and the far more violent regime of Collot and Fouché.

evidence.evidence_summary: After prolonged resistance and cooperation with royalists, the city surrendered, but Paris rejected the conciliatory model used at Caen.
The destruction decree, mass arrests, accelerated tribunal, and cannon executions transformed punishment into deliberate exemplary terror.

subjects.label: Popular radicalism: competition to define the Terror
subjects.meaning: The competition among enragés, Hébertists, commune leaders, Cordeliers, and radical deputies to claim Marat's mantle and press coercive economic and political measures.
subjects.stance: Terror was promoted through interacting popular grievance and factional entrepreneurship; it was not simply imposed from above by a single leader.

evidence.evidence_summary: After Marat's death and Roux's displacement, Hébert and Chaumette appropriated demands previously associated with the enragés.
Rival radical networks converged on maximum prices, revolutionary armies, harsher repression, and mass political action.
Commune and club leaders redirected a workers' protest into a successful march that forced immediate legislation from the Convention.

subjects.label: September Days of 1793: popular coercion of the Convention
subjects.meaning: The 4–5 September mobilization that converted wage and bread grievances into demands for revolutionary armies, faster justice, arms, and paid sectional participation.
subjects.stance: The movement appears to have begun spontaneously but was deliberately organized and amplified by Hébertist officials; its legislative success made terror the declared order of the day.

evidence.evidence_summary: Commune leaders closed workplaces, mobilized thousands, and presented subsistence and enforcement demands that the Convention accepted amid scenes of intense enthusiasm.

subjects.label: Parisian subsistence crisis as a political engine
subjects.meaning: Food scarcity, inflation, wages, price-control failures, and perceived profiteering as recurring causes of sansculotte mobilization and factional danger.
subjects.stance: Material grievance was genuine even when politicians exploited it; Doyle does not reduce popular action to manipulation alone.

evidence.evidence_summary: Food pressure helped end resistance in southern cities and shaped the political atmosphere in the capital.
Assignat depreciation, milling disruption, and sharp price increases allowed radicals to blame moderation for everyday hardship.
A workers' protest over wages and bread became the immediate vehicle for coercing new emergency measures.
A malfunctioning maximum, market scuffles, and black-market activity again made calls for insurrection dangerous in March 1794.

subjects.label: Levée en masse: mass mobilization and its limits
subjects.meaning: The August 1793 mobilization decree as both a response to sectional pressure and a practically effective but narrower measure than popular advocates imagined.
subjects.stance: Credit Carnot's implementation while preserving the distinction between effective conscription and the ideal of universal national enlistment.

evidence.evidence_summary: The decree answered sectional petitions and was implemented effectively, but authorized conscription short of the universal mobilization envisioned by radicals.

subjects.label: Law of Suspects
subjects.meaning: The September 1793 law that empowered local watch committees to arrest broadly defined enemies of liberty and made ordinary conduct and associations grounds for suspicion.
subjects.stance: Its categories were so expansive that almost anyone could be vulnerable; implementation became a central administrative mechanism of the Terror.

evidence.evidence_summary: The law authorized arrest on sweeping behavioral, associational, verbal, and status-based grounds.
Even modes of address and refusal of egalitarian speech conventions could trigger suspicion.
Watch committees enforced the law through certificates, arrest, and imprisonment on a very large scale.

subjects.label: General Maximum: nationwide price regulation
subjects.meaning: The September 1793 extension of maximum prices across necessities and its difficult transformation into a centrally administered controlled economy.
subjects.stance: The policy reduced monetary pressure and imposed real control, but enforcement was uneven, wages were largely exempt in practice, and black markets persisted.

evidence.evidence_summary: The law set ceilings for a broad range of necessities and linked overcharging to fines and suspect status.
Initial local-price formulas caused runs, uneven supply, and administrative delay, requiring rapid revision.
Central direction eventually produced national schedules and measurable economic control despite evasion and military-market distortions.

subjects.label: Revolutionary Armies: coercion, provisioning, and political control
subjects.meaning: Urban sansculotte formations used to enforce revolutionary laws, requisition provisions, identify suspects, and repress hostile districts before central government curtailed them.
subjects.stance: They were locally knowledgeable and socially rooted instruments, not a uniform national army; their coercive autonomy made them incompatible with later centralization.

evidence.evidence_summary: Popular mobilization forced the Convention to organize the armies for action against hoarders and hostile rural interests.
Ronsin, closely aligned with Hébert, received command of the Paris force.
Provincial forces recruited mainly urban married artisans and combined political intimidation, arrest, repression, and rural foraging.
Centralizing legislation abolished unofficial local forces and retained only a single closely supervised army.
The remaining Paris army was dissolved after the Hébertist prosecution, ending a major autonomous sansculotte instrument.

subjects.label: Revolutionary Tribunal: acceleration and political trials
subjects.meaning: The tribunal's expansion to process more cases and its use for predetermined trials of prominent political enemies.
subjects.stance: Separate ordinary judicial throughput from political show trials in which acquittal was effectively excluded and procedure was manipulated.

evidence.evidence_summary: Danton successfully proposed dividing the tribunal to increase its rate of adjudication.
The Girondin proceeding was deliberately shortened when defense speeches threatened to prolong a foreordained outcome.
The Committee ordered the prosecutor to secure Hébertist convictions through a transparently political case.

subjects.label: Spectacular Paris executions and the invisibility of provincial victims
subjects.meaning: The way highly visible executions of famous prisoners shaped the public image of the Terror while drawing attention away from its much larger provincial toll.
subjects.stance: Doyle calls the celebrated cases bloody but initially limited in number and warns that their fame obscured less-known victims outside Paris.

evidence.evidence_summary: Pressure for both trials overcame Robespierre's delaying efforts after an alleged rescue plot made the queen's fate unavoidable.
The queen and leading Girondins died in highly visible proceedings, while Robespierre blocked extension of the purge to all protesting deputies.

subjects.label: Enragés: suppression by victorious radicals
subjects.meaning: The arrest or disappearance of Roux, Varlet, and Leclerc after Hébertist and Montagnard rivals adopted much of their economic program.
subjects.stance: The radicals eliminated competitors whose policies they had appropriated; suppression also ended the enragés' demand to activate the democratic constitution.

evidence.evidence_summary: Leading enragés were arrested or silenced just as their economic demands became official radical policy.

subjects.label: Constitution of 1793: suspension and Revolutionary Government
subjects.meaning: The abandonment of immediate constitutional rule and declaration that France would remain under temporary Revolutionary Government until peace.
subjects.stance: Emergency government was explicitly presented as temporary, but its central direction and speed stood in sharp opposition to the democratic procedures of the suspended constitution.

evidence.evidence_summary: Saint-Just argued that emergency laws required a revolutionary form of government and secured central direction by the Committee until peace.
The later administrative system rejected decentralization and independent interpretation in favor of uniform obedience.

subjects.label: Terror: scale, geography, and social composition of victims
subjects.meaning: The distinction among official executions, other deaths under coercion, Vendéan war mortality, and the uneven social and regional distribution of victims.
subjects.stance: Use qualified estimates; reject the image of a Terror directed mainly against former privileged orders, and emphasize concentration in rebellion and frontier districts.

evidence.evidence_summary: Roughly sixteen thousand formal guillotine deaths over nine months define only the judicial core of the Terror, with relatively few early executions in Paris.
A very large share of death sentences fell in departments affected by the Vendée rebellion.
Including custody and extrajudicial deaths may approximately double the official total, while ordinary and middle-class people greatly outnumbered nobles and clergy among victims.

subjects.label: Terror: imprisonment, custody deaths, and extrajudicial killing
subjects.meaning: The broader coercive mortality beyond formal death sentences, including mass imprisonment, epidemic custody deaths, lynching, and unrecorded murder.
subjects.stance: These victims belong in an assessment of the Terror even though no court formally condemned them; retain the uncertainty of aggregate estimates.

evidence.evidence_summary: Up to hundreds of thousands were detained as suspects, overwhelming prisons and improvised facilities.
Thousands may have died in custody, while chaotic autumn violence produced additional murders without trial or reliable records.

subjects.label: Vendée: defeat of the Catholic and Royal Army
subjects.meaning: The republican counteroffensive, the rebels' northern march seeking British support, and destruction of the remaining field army at Le Mans and Savenay.
subjects.stance: The campaign's outcome combined republican reorganization with rebel command divisions, failure to exploit victories, and failed coordination with Britain.

evidence.evidence_summary: Unified republican columns defeated the rebel center at Cholet, forcing a desperate northern march toward a port and hoped-for British aid.
Poor communications and lack of siege equipment defeated the Granville strategy, and retreat ended in a bloody rout at Le Mans.
Savenay destroyed most of the remaining force and ended the large conventional phase of the Vendée war.

subjects.label: Vendée: infernal columns and republican devastation
subjects.meaning: Turreau's spring 1794 campaign of systematic burning and indiscriminate killing in the rebel heartland after the field army's defeat.
subjects.stance: Distinguish deliberate post-battle devastation from judicial Terror and preserve Doyle's strong condemnation together with uncertainty over total mortality.

evidence.evidence_summary: Columns were ordered to burn the insurgent region and kill inhabitants indiscriminately, including people loyal to the Republic.
The chapter describes rape, infanticide, and long-term demographic damage while presenting the aggregate rebel death toll as a continuing historical dispute.

subjects.label: Carrier at Nantes: shootings, noyades, and recall
subjects.meaning: Carrier's exceptionally destructive repression in an overcrowded war-zone city, including mass drownings, shootings, and later exposure for indiscriminate illegality.
subjects.stance: Place the violence in the context of real insurgent danger and local fear without excusing it; distinguish popular acquiescence from proof of legality or necessity.

evidence.evidence_summary: Special courts imposed thousands of capital sentences, while overloaded prisons and provisioning pressures helped produce mass drownings and shootings.
Many local citizens accepted severe methods because they believed a rebel victory would bring their own massacre.
Reports of indiscriminate repression and disregard for legal forms made Carrier an early casualty of the center's effort to curb autonomous terror.

subjects.label: Representatives on mission: autonomy, regional variation, and recall
subjects.meaning: The extensive discretionary power exercised by deputies in the provinces, producing outcomes from conciliation to mass repression before the center restricted and recalled them.
subjects.stance: Regional Terror cannot be explained as uniform execution of a single Parisian plan; individual choices and local conditions were often decisive.

evidence.evidence_summary: Couthon's preference for conciliation at Lyons was overridden by a central demand for exemplary vengeance and by replacement personnel.
Tallien and Ysabeau used violent rhetoric in Bordeaux while administering comparatively limited repression.
During autumn 1793 representatives interpreted their missions freely, helping make Terror decentralized and inconsistent.
The centralizing law and later investigations broke their independent authority despite resistance and delayed compliance.

subjects.label: Terror: anarchic and decentralized phase
subjects.meaning: The autumn 1793 phase in which representatives, revolutionary armies, local committees, and improvised bodies applied terror with little uniform central control.
subjects.stance: This phase was violent and locally variable; calling it anarchic describes fragmented authority, not absence of institutions or policy.

evidence.evidence_summary: Provincial armies multiplied and representatives exercised broad discretion with limited direction from Paris.
Geographic quiet or violence could depend heavily on the personal program of an individual representative.
The Law of 14 Frimaire is presented as the transition away from autonomous armies and proconsular power toward central government.

subjects.label: Watch committees and certificates of civisme
subjects.meaning: Local committees that identified suspects, administered the Law of Suspects, and used civic certificates as combined identity and political-reliability documents.
subjects.stance: Their local knowledge made them effective instruments of mass suspicion; unlike improvised bodies, they survived centralization because national policy depended on them.

evidence.evidence_summary: Committees used intimate local knowledge to identify suspects and required widely applicable certificates of civic reliability.
They remained active under centralization because enforcement of the suspect law still depended on them and they reported to the security committee.

subjects.label: Fouché in the Nièvre: civic religion and religious terror
subjects.meaning: Fouché's locally initiated program against public Christianity, clerical celibacy, religious symbolism, and burial belief.
subjects.stance: The program arose from Fouché's interpretation of clerical power in the Vendée, not from prior Convention authorization, and became a model for wider dechristianization.

evidence.evidence_summary: Fouché transformed a quiet department into a center of religious terror after concluding that Christianity could not coexist with the Revolution.
He promoted universal morality, restricted worship to private space, attacked clerical separation, and replaced Christian burial symbolism with secular doctrine.

subjects.label: Dechristianization: origins, spread, and limits
subjects.meaning: The decentralized movement to remove Catholic worship, personnel, symbols, calendars, and institutions from public life during the Terror.
subjects.stance: It was neither originally authorized nor fully controlled by the Convention; it spread through representatives, armies, clubs, and local authorities and eventually exhausted its available targets.

evidence.evidence_summary: Representatives, revolutionary armies, and local activists attacked clerical status, church property, symbols, and public observance without initial national authorization.
Parisian authorities institutionalized church closure, civic festivals, clerical renunciation, and the replacement of Christian space with revolutionary symbolism.
Despite national warnings and a decree protecting worship, the movement spread widely before running out of churches, clergy, and furnishings to attack.
Its disorder became an important reason for the Committee to impose a tighter chain of authority.

subjects.label: Republican calendar: secularization of public time
subjects.meaning: The October 1793 calendar that dated years from the Republic, renamed months seasonally, replaced seven-day weeks with décades, and displaced Sundays.
subjects.stance: Although not itself identical with dechristianization, its timing encouraged representatives to intensify the attack on Christian practice.

evidence.evidence_summary: The new system reset historical time around the Republic and substituted ten-day cycles for Christian weekly observance.

subjects.label: Paris Commune: Temple of Reason and official dechristianization
subjects.meaning: The Commune's adoption of dechristianization through removal of religious and royal imagery, clerical renunciation, church closure, and the Notre-Dame festival of Reason.
subjects.stance: The ceremonies were carefully staged but are treated as undignified political spectacle whose apparent official encouragement magnified a decentralized movement.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Commune ordered symbolic removals, promoted clerical resignation, closed churches, and staged a civic spectacle in the converted cathedral.

subjects.label: Clergy under the Terror: coercion, deportation, and renunciation
subjects.meaning: The extension of suspicion and coercion to constitutional as well as refractory clergy through denunciation, deportation, execution, forced resignation, and pressure to marry.
subjects.stance: Do not conflate all anticlerical policy with formal execution policy or assume renunciations were voluntary; many were produced by intimidation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Non-juring priests formed a substantial share of those drowned at Nantes on suspicion of sustaining insurgent religious zeal.
Representatives demanded public abjuration and treated even constitutional clerical status as suspect.
Paris combined harsher deportation law with theatrical episcopal and priestly renunciations.
By spring 1794 large numbers of priests had been pressured to abandon status, and thousands had married as the strongest confirmation of renunciation.

subjects.label: Popular resistance to dechristianization
subjects.meaning: Rural and small-town resistance generated when anticlerical activists attacked elected clergy, Sunday worship, and familiar religious practice.
subjects.stance: The Brie rising shows that indiscriminate anticlerical zeal could create new enemies and threaten strategically important supply routes.

evidence.evidence_summary: Peasants attacked a local club and armed themselves in defense of priests, Mass, and customary holy days until republican forces restored order.

subjects.label: Robespierre: religion, the Supreme Being, and freedom of cults
subjects.meaning: Robespierre's argument that public morality required religious belief and that atheistic persecution endangered rather than secured the Revolution.
subjects.stance: He opposed dechristianizing excess and defended legal freedom of worship without restoring Catholic establishment or endorsing superstition.

evidence.evidence_summary: He warned that atheistic zeal was itself fanatical, affirmed popular belief in a Supreme Being, and secured both central warnings and a decree against coerced worship restrictions.

subjects.label: Law of 14 Frimaire: centralization of Revolutionary Government
subjects.meaning: The December 1793 law that created a hierarchical chain of authority centered on the governing committees and demanded uniform execution of revolutionary law.
subjects.stance: It ended the principle of autonomous local interpretation and established France's strongest central government since 1787, but implementation took months.

evidence.evidence_summary: The law placed internal administration and police under the Committee, reduced ministers to transmission, prohibited local reinterpretation, and reorganized reporting.
It marked the intended end of autonomous terror and proconsular rule and created unusually strong central authority, though compliance was delayed.

subjects.label: Revolutionary Government: districts, communes, and national agents
subjects.meaning: The administrative machinery that bypassed conservative departments, assigned execution to districts and communes, and monitored each locality through centrally appointed national agents.
subjects.stance: The arrangement sought speed, uniformity, and independent reporting, leaving departments only routine functions rather than eliminating all local administration.

evidence.evidence_summary: Local councils reported directly to Paris through a ten-day rhythm while national agents supplied separate oversight and departments lost most policy authority.

subjects.label: Revolutionary versus constitutional government
subjects.meaning: The theoretical distinction between peaceful constitutional rule that preserves an established republic and extraordinary wartime government intended to found one.
subjects.stance: Record this as Robespierre's explicit justification for emergency centralization, not as a neutral timeless definition of democracy.

evidence.evidence_summary: Robespierre contrasted the preservation of a peaceful republic with the extraordinary activity required to establish liberty during war.

subjects.label: Centralization: delayed compliance and representative resistance
subjects.meaning: The months-long struggle to make the Law of 14 Frimaire effective against provincial armies, continuing dechristianization, and representatives unwilling to surrender autonomy.
subjects.stance: Do not treat passage of the law as instant administrative transformation; local defiance persisted and required recall and investigation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Provincial forces and religious attacks continued, while Javogues openly rejected the law's applicability until recalled after prolonged defiance.

subjects.label: Subsistence Commission and Robert Lindet
subjects.meaning: The national agency placed under Committee supervision to direct bulk purchasing, grants, trade, distribution, and the detailed schedule of maximum prices.
subjects.stance: Doyle portrays Lindet as the central organizer of economic mobilization, comparable in administrative importance to Carnot's military role.

evidence.evidence_summary: Under Lindet the commission gained broad coordinating powers and produced a national price schedule for necessities.

subjects.label: Controlled economy: black markets and assignat recovery
subjects.meaning: The partial economic stabilization achieved through price and supply controls despite evasion, administrative gaps, and preferential military purchasing.
subjects.stance: The controls were neither complete failures nor comprehensive successes; their clearest short-term effect was a marked but temporary improvement in paper currency value.

evidence.evidence_summary: Black markets and above-maximum military purchases persisted, yet reduced currency demand allowed issuance to slow and the assignat to rise sharply before later decline.

subjects.label: Forced loan on the rich, 1793
subjects.meaning: The steeply progressive levy on higher incomes that removed depreciated assignats from circulation and symbolized class-directed emergency finance.
subjects.stance: Its nominal severity was softened by payment in depreciated currency and uneven local implementation, but the wealthy remembered it as vindictive class legislation.

evidence.evidence_summary: The measure emerged from earlier sansculotte pressure and became one component of arresting currency decline.
A confiscatory-looking income scale was implemented unevenly and paid in depreciated notes, but carried powerful class-punitive meaning.

subjects.label: Laws of Ventôse: proposed redistribution to indigent patriots
subjects.meaning: Saint-Just's decrees to sequester and redistribute property of recognized enemies to approved poor patriots through local lists and popular commissions.
subjects.stance: The measures were radical in language but poorly conceived, weakly supported within government, and implemented only minimally; do not present them as a completed land reform.

evidence.evidence_summary: The decrees envisioned identifying enemies and transferring their goods to approved poor patriots, but administrative confusion and committee reluctance left little accomplished.

subjects.label: Terror: emergent, uncontrolled, and self-perpetuating system
subjects.meaning: Doyle's interpretation that no one designed a complete system of terror, that crisis produced it through cumulative measures, and that fear made it difficult to criticize or stop.
subjects.stance: Preserve the distinction between absence of a single founding design and the real agency of officials who later organized, defended, or intensified coercion.

evidence.evidence_summary: A retrospective deputy's claim that circumstances created terror frames a system that no actor fully controlled and few could safely criticize.
Military and political recovery encouraged demands for moderation, but denunciation made restraint personally dangerous.
Removing popular radical leaders did not end terror; government control prepared a still harsher phase.

subjects.label: Indulgents: campaign for clemency and attack on excess
subjects.meaning: The loose alignment around Danton and Desmoulins seeking reduced bloodshed, relief from wrongful arrest, and criticism of provincial terror and dechristianization.
subjects.stance: The Indulgents were not a coherent innocent opposition: corruption allegations and personal loyalties compromised them and helped end Robespierre's temporary support.

evidence.evidence_summary: Dantonist criticism of representative abuses helped accompany the central campaign to reduce provincial autonomy.
Danton called for less bloodshed and Desmoulins began a paper attacking the Cordeliers' new terrorist leadership.
Fabre's proven involvement in financial fraud discredited the movement's moral attack on Hébertist corruption.
Danton's demand to free Fabre cast doubt on whether indulgence reflected public principle or protection of friends.

subjects.label: Robespierre: moderation, centralization, and factional realignment
subjects.meaning: Robespierre's temporary alignment with Dantonist moderation, advocacy of centralized control, and later abandonment of the Indulgents after corruption revelations.
subjects.stance: Avoid the simple image of an unchanging architect of maximum terror: his position shifted, but suspicion and demands for virtue also helped authorize later purges.

evidence.evidence_summary: He opposed unnecessary executions and dechristianization, defended Danton, and supported stronger central government as a restraint on excess.
Fabre's exposure ended his experiment with the Indulgents and redirected suspicion toward their wider network.
His return from illness stiffened the Committee immediately before it moved against the Hébertists.

subjects.label: Danton: emergency mobilization and politics of indulgence
subjects.meaning: Danton's role in winning emergency measures in September and later advocating moderation while defending compromised associates.
subjects.stance: His contribution was substantial but politically ambiguous: advocacy of clemency cannot be separated from friendship with Fabre and earlier support for coercive institutions.

evidence.evidence_summary: He sponsored revolutionary-army, arms-production, tribunal, and paid-assembly measures during the September confrontation.
He publicly urged less bloodshed and cooperated in creating stronger central administration.
His isolated defense of the arrested Fabre tied personal loyalty to the factional crisis.

subjects.label: Desmoulins and the Vieux Cordelier
subjects.meaning: Desmoulins's newspaper campaign against terror, dechristianization, wrongful detention, and the Hébertist leadership of the Cordeliers.
subjects.stance: The paper became the voice of indulgence with Robespierre's initial blessing, but its allies' corruption and escalating polemic undermined the campaign.

evidence.evidence_summary: The paper invoked the older Cordeliers tradition to criticize the club's current terrorist and dechristianizing masters.
Its comparisons with ancient despotism and attacks on Lyons fed the clemency campaign before Fabre's scandal broke its alliance with Robespierre.

subjects.label: Indies Company scandal: corruption and factional politics
subjects.meaning: The fraudulent manipulation of the former Indies Company's liquidation and its use to implicate deputies and reorganize factional alignments.
subjects.stance: Financial corruption was real, but expansive claims that it proved a coordinated counter-revolutionary conspiracy were not established.

evidence.evidence_summary: Chabot alleged that corrupt deputies had manipulated company liquidation and entrapped patriots, while investigators suspected self-protection.
Fabre's documented involvement discredited the Indulgents and led to his arrest despite their attacks on others' corruption.

subjects.label: Foreign-plot rhetoric and factional prosecution
subjects.meaning: The use of alleged British, Austrian, or other foreign direction to connect corruption, food shortages, insurrection, and political opposition into prosecutable conspiracies.
subjects.stance: Record the allegations as claims. Doyle accepts that some agents and intrigues existed but regards the Hébertist trial case as constructed and its broad plot theory implausible.

evidence.evidence_summary: Robespierre found a sweeping counter-revolutionary theory plausible because real intrigue and financial fraud gave it partial foundations.
Saint-Just and the tribunal joined faction, famine, insurrection, prison violence, and foreign nationals into a case designed to secure conviction.

subjects.label: Collot d'Herbois: Lyonnais repression and defense of terror
subjects.meaning: Collot's movement from severe representative at Lyons to influential defender of terrorist allies and opponent of the Indulgent challenge within Paris.
subjects.stance: His self-protective return helped re-legitimate terror and polarize politics, but he later closed ranks with the Committee against uncontrolled Hébertist insurrection.

evidence.evidence_summary: He arrived with Fouché to replace Couthon's restraint and accelerate exemplary punishment at Lyons.
His forceful defense of Ronsin revived the terrorist faction and helped abolish the proposed justice committee.
After protecting his own position, he urged unity behind established government rather than a new purge.

subjects.label: Hébertists: failed insurrection and political execution
subjects.meaning: The revived Cordeliers campaign for a new purge, its failure to mobilize Paris beyond one section, and the Committee's preemptive arrest and execution of Hébertist leaders.
subjects.stance: The alleged conspiracy charges were manufactured for a political result, yet the movement's organizational weakness and reckless insurrectionary rhetoric were real.

evidence.evidence_summary: Returning provincial terrorists and Cordeliers leaders called for a new insurrection, but only section Marat declared itself in uprising.
After renewing its mandate the Committee arrested Hébert, Vincent, Ronsin, Momoro, and associates and sent them to a politically predetermined trial.
Popular hostility and the failure of other sections to mobilize left self-proclaimed sansculotte champions without an effective defense.

subjects.label: Sansculottes: exhaustion, institutional absorption, and political decline
subjects.meaning: The weakening of autonomous sansculotte politics as prolonged mobilization produced fatigue, core demands were enacted, and experienced militants entered paid or administrative roles.
subjects.stance: Their abandonment of the Hébertists reflected more than deception: many believed the government was implementing their program and defending a Republic that was winning.

evidence.evidence_summary: Most sections ignored the insurrectionary appeal and ordinary Parisians accepted the official allegations against radical leaders.
After two years of strain, many militants saw their principal economic and coercive demands enacted and supported the government that enforced them.
Committee service and paid sectional attendance drew experienced activists into the state, while alternative societies could not restore autonomous power.

subjects.label: Paris Commune purge and transfer of Terror to government
subjects.meaning: The destruction of the Commune as an independent popular institution, dissolution of the Revolutionary Army, and transfer of coercive power into the central state.
subjects.stance: This ended the sansculottes as an autonomous force but did not end terror; the chapter's closing paradox is that centralized governmental terror was about to become worse.

evidence.evidence_summary: Chaumette and others were executed, the Commune's personnel were purged into obedience, and Ronsin's army was abolished.
Popular control of terror ended, but the resulting government monopoly did not bring moderation and instead opened a more intense phase.

subjects.label: Central review of provincial Terror: Tallien, Carrier, and Jullien
subjects.meaning: The use of Jullien as Robespierre's investigator and the recall or supplementation of representatives suspected of either excessive or insufficient repression.
subjects.stance: Central review was politically contingent and briefly sought limits on excess; it did not amount to a stable general policy of clemency.

evidence.evidence_summary: Jullien was sent to Bordeaux after exposing abuses at Nantes and then sharply increased executions in a city whose earlier repression was judged too mild.
His reports on unlawful indiscrimination helped bring Carrier back to Paris as official policy shifted toward restricting representatives.
Robespierre-backed missions against Carrier and Tallien formed part of the wider effort to end proconsular autonomy.

subjects.label: Bonaparte at the siege of Toulon
subjects.meaning: Captain Bonaparte's artillery role in taking the heights that made coalition evacuation of Toulon unavoidable.
subjects.stance: Treat this as a significant tactical episode within Toulon's recovery, not as the chapter's explanation of the whole siege or later Napoleonic destiny.

evidence.evidence_summary: Bonaparte's guns helped clear the key harbor heights, exposing the coalition fleet and forcing evacuation.

subjects.label: Revolutionary language as a test of civic conformity
subjects.meaning: The expectation that everyday address use egalitarian revolutionary forms and the treatment of older deferential language as evidence of suspect politics.
subjects.stance: This is an illustrative social extension of the suspect regime, not proof that linguistic nonconformity always produced formal prosecution.

evidence.evidence_summary: Use of deferential rather than egalitarian forms of address became an automatic marker of possible political unreliability.

subjects.label: Hébert and Père Duchesne: radical leadership and downfall
subjects.meaning: Hébert's ascent as the leading popular journalist after Marat, promotion of coercive economic and political measures, and eventual execution after failed insurrectionary maneuvering.
subjects.stance: He was an influential opportunistic spokesman rather than the sole author of sansculotte demands; his movement's claims to represent the people were disproved by its isolation in March 1794.

evidence.evidence_summary: His newspaper became Paris's dominant popular paper and helped transfer enragé demands into a new radical leadership.
He used economic hardship and resentment of moderation to press the Jacobins toward renewed popular action.
He joined calls for a new purge but failed to extend the uprising beyond the Cordeliers' immediate base.
He was condemned in a political conspiracy trial and died without the popular mobilization his faction expected.

subjects.label: Chaumette: subsistence mobilization, dechristianization, and Commune purge
subjects.meaning: Chaumette's role as Commune procurator in the September mobilization, adoption of dechristianization, guarded response to the March uprising, and later execution.
subjects.stance: His trajectory connects popular pressure and Commune power but also shows political caution when the Hébertist insurrection failed to spread.

evidence.evidence_summary: He led the mass delegation that demanded subsistence enforcement and revolutionary armies.
After observing Fouché's program, he helped make dechristianization official Commune policy.
He received the isolated section Marat uprising cautiously when no other section followed.
His later arrest and execution formed part of reducing the Commune to obedience.

subjects.label: Saint-Just: Revolutionary Government, Ventôse, and anti-faction policy
subjects.meaning: Saint-Just's role in defining emergency government, proposing redistributive Ventôse measures, and framing factional opposition as foreign-inspired resistance to popular sovereignty.
subjects.stance: His interventions combined constitutional theory, underdeveloped social radicalism, and political prosecution; they should not be collapsed into a single consistent economic program.

evidence.evidence_summary: He justified central emergency direction as necessary for revolutionary law and secured government until peace.
He proposed sequestering enemy property for poor patriots without fully resolving implementation or winning strong committee commitment.
His speech condemned faction and insurrection in sweeping terms that prepared the Hébertist arrests without naming concrete offenders.

subjects.label: Billaud-Varenne: radical legislation and central authority
subjects.meaning: Billaud-Varenne's promotion of punitive economic law, revolutionary-army action, Committee radicalization, and defense of central authority against both indulgence and faction.
subjects.stance: He consistently favored coercive energy, but his later defense of the established committees distinguished centralized terror from uncontrolled popular purges.

evidence.evidence_summary: He stood out among Montagnards for punitive economic legislation and rejection of conciliatory caution.
He sponsored the revolutionary-army measure and then joined the Committee during the September radicalization.
During centralization debates he pressed for an even cleaner concentration of executive authority.
With Collot he helped defeat the Indulgent justice committee inside the governing coalition.

subjects.label: Marie-Antoinette: trial and execution
subjects.meaning: The former queen's transfer to trial and execution after discovery of a rescue plot made further delay politically impossible.
subjects.stance: Treat the proceeding as a politically demanded exemplary trial whose outcome was effectively predetermined, not as an ordinary neutral prosecution.

evidence.evidence_summary: Robespierre delayed the demanded prosecution until news of an attempted rescue made a trial politically unavoidable.
Her highly visible execution became one of the first defining spectacles of the Terror.

subjects.label: Girondins: show trial, executions, and fugitive deaths
subjects.meaning: The compressed show trial and execution of leading Girondins, imprisonment of protest signatories, and deaths of fugitives outside Paris.
subjects.stance: The central proceeding was designed to avoid prolonged defense, but Robespierre resisted extending capital prosecution to every deputy associated with the purge protest.

evidence.evidence_summary: Popular and legislative pressure sent the detained Girondins to trial while efforts to identify advocates of mercy were partly resisted.
The trial was cut short, leading figures were executed, and several fugitives later died by execution or suicide.

subjects.label: Carnot: military organization and mass mobilization
subjects.meaning: Carnot's addition to the Committee as a military specialist and his practical organization of the levée en masse and wartime resources.
subjects.stance: Doyle credits administrative effectiveness while noting that the mobilization decree remained narrower than popular dreams of universal enlistment.

evidence.evidence_summary: Carnot joined the Committee as an experienced military technocrat during its turn toward effective national leadership.
His prose and implementation made the mass-mobilization decree spectacularly effective despite its limited legal scope.

subjects.label: Couthon at Lyons: conciliation rejected
subjects.meaning: Couthon's attempt to adapt the successful Caen model of courts, selective demolition, and clemency to Lyons before requesting transfer.
subjects.stance: His restraint demonstrates that exceptionally violent repression was a contested policy choice, not an automatic consequence of every rebel city's surrender.

evidence.evidence_summary: Couthon favored the conciliatory approach used in Normandy even though Paris regarded Lyons as uniquely culpable.
He began limited courts and demolition but withdrew rather than execute the comprehensive vengeance demanded from the center.

subjects.label: Chalier: martyrdom and justification for vengeance at Lyons
subjects.meaning: The execution of the Lyonnais Jacobin Chalier and its later use as evidence that the city deserved punishment more severe than other Federalist centers.
subjects.stance: His death mattered politically as a martyr narrative and as one element in Paris's differentiated judgment of Lyons.

evidence.evidence_summary: Lyons's execution of Chalier signaled continued defiance during the Republic's crisis.
The murder of a Jacobin martyr helped distinguish Lyons from centers where conciliation remained acceptable.

subjects.label: Ronsin: Revolutionary Army command and Hébertist downfall
subjects.meaning: Ronsin's leadership of the Paris Revolutionary Army, collaboration with Collot at Lyons, role in revived factional agitation, and execution with Hébert.
subjects.stance: His trajectory connects provincial coercion to Parisian faction, but the prosecution's claims of a coordinated famine and massacre conspiracy were manufactured.

evidence.evidence_summary: His close alignment with Hébert helped him secure command of the Paris Revolutionary Army.
His arrest after returning from Lyons prompted Collot's forceful defense of terrorist methods.
He was condemned and executed with the Hébertist leadership in a predetermined political trial.

subjects.label: Vincent: war-ministry radicalism and factional agitation
subjects.meaning: Vincent's position in the war ministry, arrests and release, and renewed demand for purges that helped precipitate the Hébertist prosecution.
subjects.stance: He was a genuine advocate of further purges, but the comprehensive criminal plot alleged at trial was not demonstrated.

evidence.evidence_summary: The war-ministry official was arrested after hinting at a new purge of advocates of indulgence.
After release he rejected reconciliation and continued demanding purges, helping renew the factional crisis.

subjects.label: Committee of General Security: surveillance and factional detention
subjects.meaning: The parallel governing committee responsible for security oversight, watch-committee reporting, and politically consequential detention decisions.
subjects.stance: Its actions sometimes diverged from Robespierre's factional expectations; it was an institution with its own members and suspicions, not merely an arm of one individual.

evidence.evidence_summary: The centralized watch-committee network reported to the security committee.
Its members imprisoned Chabot after interpreting his conspiracy disclosure as an attempt to save himself.
It released Vincent and Ronsin for lack of evidence, a decision that immediately revived factional conflict.

subjects.label: Maximum wages: non-enforcement and political limits
subjects.meaning: The wage-ceiling provision of the General Maximum that remained largely unenforced because it required new administration and threatened the Commune's wage-earning base.
subjects.stance: Do not infer that price control and wage control were implemented equally; political dependence on sansculotte labor made the distinction substantial.

evidence.evidence_summary: Authorities largely avoided the wage ceiling because enforcement was administratively costly and politically dangerous among Parisian workers already earning above it.

subjects.label: Hoarding and speculation: criminalization and enforcement
subjects.meaning: The treatment of hoarders, speculators, and noncompliant producers as political enemies through capital law, suspect status, searches, and armed provisioning.
subjects.stance: Economic coercion responded to genuine supply problems but also converted market behavior and rural resistance into categories of political disloyalty.

evidence.evidence_summary: Radicals demanded harsher action against hoarders and speculators as the central answer to shortages and price rises.
The September movement demanded armed enforcement in the countryside against those accused of withholding provisions.
Severe laws and informal armed terror failed to eliminate black markets under the expanding control system.

subjects.label: Freedom of cults decree: legal restraint versus local practice
subjects.meaning: The Convention's December reaffirmation of religious freedom and prohibition on coercing worship amid continued church closure and harassment.
subjects.stance: The decree marked a real central limit but initially lacked the reach to reverse a movement already spreading through local authorities.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Convention formally barred threats or violence against worship after central warnings about counterproductive persecution.
Local closures nevertheless continued because the central government could not yet reverse the momentum of Parisian and provincial zeal.

subjects.label: Terror in comparative European perspective
subjects.meaning: The comparison of French Terror mortality with contemporary mass killing elsewhere in Europe to qualify claims of unique bloodiness.
subjects.stance: The comparison contextualizes scale without minimizing French victims or making unlike events analytically identical.

evidence.evidence_summary: Doyle compares the broader estimated French toll with shorter but similarly destructive violence in Ireland and Warsaw.

subjects.label: Paid sectional attendance and the forty-sou patriots
subjects.meaning: Danton's scheme to pay workers for twice-weekly sectional attendance and its later effect in replacing permanent popular sessions with scheduled, state-supported participation.
subjects.stance: The reform widened practical access for wage earners but also helped domesticate and professionalize the sansculotte movement; retain both effects.

evidence.evidence_summary: Payment was presented as enabling working people to attend fixed meetings without sacrificing their livelihood.
Critics later saw the paid schedule as a cheap surrender of permanent assembly, while it drew activists into regularized state-supported roles.

subjects.label: Republican victories and pressure to moderate the Terror
subjects.meaning: The easing of the military and civil-war emergency in late 1793 as the condition that made demands for less violent government politically possible.
subjects.stance: Improved security generated pressure for moderation but did not automatically end the Terror because institutions, suspicions, and factional interests had become self-sustaining.

evidence.evidence_summary: Victories over coalition armies, recapture of rebel cities, and defeat of the Vendéans reduced the apparent necessity for maximum coercion.
Political pressure for a less savage regime rose as the emergency lifted, even though denunciation still made criticism hazardous.

subjects.label: Committee of justice: proposed review of wrongful arrest
subjects.meaning: Robespierre's short-lived proposal for a body to investigate unjust detentions during the Indulgent campaign.
subjects.stance: Its creation signaled a real moment of concern about excess, but rapid abolition by terrorist members shows the fragility of that restraint.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Convention created the review body at Robespierre's urging, but Collot and Billaud soon secured its abolition.

subjects.label: Tallien at Bordeaux: moderation, suspicion, and recall
subjects.meaning: Tallien's entry into Bordeaux, comparatively limited local Terror, compromised reputation through elite associations, and later recall under central suspicion.
subjects.stance: His bloodthirsty rhetoric did not match the relative moderation of practice; personal relationships contributed to suspicion but should not substitute for measured outcomes.

evidence.evidence_summary: Bordeaux's earlier propaganda and hesitant surrender shaped the punitive expectations confronting its representatives.
Tallien's commission executed comparatively few people, while his relationship with Thérèse Cabarrus and elite contacts fed accusations of softness.
Central investigation eventually brought his recall as part of breaking representatives' autonomous authority.

subjects.label: Jullien: investigation and recalibration of provincial repression
subjects.meaning: The young Robespierrist emissary who exposed Carrier's abuses, scrutinized other representatives, and temporarily intensified a Bordeaux Terror judged too mild.
subjects.stance: His missions show that central intervention could curb excessive illegality or demand harsher repression depending on the locality and political moment.

evidence.evidence_summary: His success investigating Nantes led to a Bordeaux appointment where executions increased sharply over a short period.
He accepted denunciations of Carrier and reported indiscriminate action and disregard for law to the center.
His missions formed part of Robespierre's campaign to investigate questionable representatives and subordinate them to central authority.

subjects.label: Revolutionary renaming as symbolic punishment
subjects.meaning: The attempted erasure or recoding of rebel places through names that proclaimed revolutionary victory and civic disgrace.
subjects.stance: Renaming was unevenly pursued and should be treated as a symbolic adjunct to repression rather than evidence that the old names disappeared in practice.

evidence.evidence_summary: Paris ordered Lyons's name erased and replaced as part of exemplary civic annihilation.
Renaming at Toulon and Marseilles varied in seriousness, reflecting different levels of intended punishment.

subjects.label: Foreign nationals in the Hébertist show trial
subjects.meaning: The inclusion of conspicuous foreign-born defendants, including Clootz, to give visual and rhetorical substance to the alleged foreign conspiracy.
subjects.stance: Their presence served prosecutorial theater and did not independently prove foreign direction of the Hébertist faction.

evidence.evidence_summary: A group of colorful foreign-born defendants was executed with Hébertist leaders to reinforce the prosecution's foreign-plot narrative.

exclusions.decision: No source-subject evidence locator is assigned to context-only pages.
exclusions.rationale: The pages were read for continuity but belong to adjacent chunks under the frozen ownership manifest.

exclusions.decision: Intermediate towns and route points are not each promoted to separate subjects.
exclusions.rationale: Places such as La Réole, Coron, Torfou, Granville, Angers, Laval, and Cholet function chiefly as stages in larger Federalist or Vendéan narratives; the larger campaign subjects preserve access.

exclusions.decision: Unnamed witnesses, soldiers, and the retrospectively quoted deputy are not independent person subjects.
exclusions.rationale: Their testimony supplies evidence for violence or interpretation but the source does not treat their biographies or independent significance.

exclusions.decision: Individual price, vote, execution, and mortality figures are retained in evidence but not indexed as separate concepts.
exclusions.rationale: The indexable subjects are the economic, judicial, and demographic arguments the figures support.

exclusions.decision: Revolutionary place-renaming is not promoted to a standalone subject in this chunk.
exclusions.rationale: Names such as Ville Affranchie, Port-de-la-Montagne, and Vengé are preserved as access terms under the relevant repression subjects rather than fragmented into trivial entries.

exclusions.decision: Absent endnotes are outside the discovery denominator.
exclusions.rationale: The supplied restricted PDF contains note markers but no note text; no subject or evidence claim was inferred from unavailable notes.

alternatives: Parisian label for heterogeneous provincial resistance
uncertainties.judgment: Use the conventional label but preserve quotation or qualification and regional differences.

alternatives: broader total including custody and extrajudicial deaths
uncertainties.judgment: Retain each denominator and Doyle's qualifying language; do not present one figure as an uncontested total.
Record severe long-term demographic destruction while labeling the numerical estimate as debated.
Use an approximate rather than exact total and keep the method distinct from formal court executions.

alternatives: political construction built from real intrigue, corruption, and unrelated actors
uncertainties.judgment: Index the allegations and rhetoric, not the sweeping conspiracy as fact.
Doyle favors emergent origins while also identifying later decisions that centralized and intensified terror.
Use the documented cleaned-body count of 11,621 words; minor extractor/tokenization variations should not alter substantive discovery.

alternatives: body plus notes if a complete edition becomes available
uncertainties.judgment: The present artifact covers every supplied body page but makes no claim about subjects treated only in absent notes.

discovery_assessment.completeness_statement: All owned pages and all declared context pages were read. Subjects were selected for substantive independent retrieval value under the scholarly-readership policy, without a density quota.
